ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: The primary coil of an ideal transformer is connected to the sinusoidal alternating voltage shown in Figure A. The number of turns of the transformer primary coil is n1=270 turns. P is a sliding contact on the secondary coil. When P is at the position shown in Figure B, the number of turns of the secondary coil connected into the circuit is n2=135 turns, capacitor C is just not broken down, lamp L just emits light normally, and R is a sliding rheostat. Which of the following judgments is correct
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: The breakdown voltage of the capacitor is 11V

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: Figure A is a sinusoidal graph of the alternating voltage u connected to the primary coil changing with time t; the vertical axis is labeled u/V, the dashed lines mark the maximum value as 22√2 V and the minimum value as -22√2 V, and times such as 0.01 s and 0.02 s can be seen on the horizontal axis. Figure B is an ideal transformer and the external circuit of the secondary coil; the primary coil is connected to the AC power source u, and the secondary coil has a sliding contact P; in the external circuit on the right, capacitor C is connected between the upper and lower output wires, and lamp L and sliding rheostat R are also connected in this output circuit. Reasoning: From Figure A, read the peak voltage of the primary coil as Um1=22√2 V, therefore the effective value of the primary coil voltage is U1=Um1/√2=22 V. The problem gives the number of turns of the primary coil n1=270 turns, and when P is at the position in Figure B, the number of turns of the secondary coil connected into the circuit is n2=135 turns. An ideal transformer satisfies U2/U1=n2/n1, so the effective value of the secondary coil output voltage is U2=22×135/270=11 V. In Figure B, capacitor C is directly connected across the two ends of the secondary coil output terminals, therefore UC=U2=11 V. Since the problem states that capacitor C is just not broken down, its breakdown voltage equals the voltage across its two ends at this time, namely 11 V.
